decisions.what: Re-aimed the brief's three headings AWAY from 'harden tests' and onto reducing the guard layer's maintenance tax, on measured grounds
decisions.why: Stress-test verdict RESHAPE (confidence 8). Coverage is 100% line / 100% func / 98.44% branch with the single miss classified BOUNDARY, so a new product test would be written to a number rather than to a defect (L-031 inverted: the measurement says there are no untested surfaces). Meanwhile test/ is 4409 lines against a 594-line program and 3286 of those lines guard DOCUMENTS. The toy version of this brief is 'add more guards that read the README' — and that is exactly what runs #2-#6 built.

decisions.what: Retired run #6's '>= 121 tests' invariant and replaced it with a detection floor
decisions.why: A test-COUNT floor can only ever be satisfied by growth, so it makes consolidation a spec violation regardless of whether detection is preserved. It is the specific mechanism that kept KI-R6-3 open for two runs. Naming the ratchet and replacing it is the highest-value change available inside this brief.

decisions.what: Acted on the taste judge's finding BEFORE lock rather than merely recording it: R-1's mutation set was bounded by a stated generation rule, capped at 30, given an identity control, and required to ship as a rerunnable harness
decisions.why: The judge was right that the draft asserted a universal claim over an unbounded mutation universe and asked only that the matrix be 'published'. A floor nobody can re-run is not a floor, and run #8 would have inherited a report instead of a check. This is the one thing the taste gate exists to catch, and it caught it.

decisions.what: Planned this run as ONE session rather than 3-5 cycles, and said so in the spec
decisions.why: runs/allocator.json at kickoff: weekly_used_pct 100.0, week_resets_at 2026-08-24T05:00Z — 10.5h AFTER this run's stop_at. The ENTIRE run window sits inside an exhausted weekly limit. KI-R6-6 measured the cost of ignoring that: 503 of 504 pacer-spawned cycles died on HTTP 429 in ~380ms before their first turn. Planning for one session is the honest read of the measurement, not pessimism.

Two guards in test/readme-tags.test.js now read the same "Tags on exactly one entry" table row (the renamed multi/single-entry test and the structural replacement for the retired co-occurrence guard). This redundancy was INDUCED BY THE CONDUCTOR's dispatch, which mandated both the re-anchor and a no-shrink floor; the builder disclosed it rather than hiding it. Harmless but not coverage — a candidate consolidation once the Q-5 floor is not the binding constraint.

The README Node-support matrix can still be falsified WHOLESALE: gate cell C7 (cycle 4) changed all four rows together to a self-consistent falsehood (200 tests, 198 pass, 0 fail, 2 skipped) and test/readme-matrix-consistency.test.js stayed SILENT at 5 pass / 0 fail. Per-row arithmetic and cross-row agreement catch a single bad row, a transcription slip, or a partial edit — not a lie told consistently. Closing it requires an anchor outside the document (live network provenance, which would skip in the shallow-CI environment the table describes; or a committed machine-readable CI artifact, which changes what CI is responsible for). Operator's call — Q-9.

docs/node-support-citation-history.md PARAPHRASES the rewritten citation-selection rule instead of quoting the README's wording, and the paraphrase is a different rule: it selects 'the most recent run whose cited commit's src/bin/test/.github content is byte-identical to this tree', which on this tree selects 3a5d6e3 @ run 32405575919 (more recent, and `git diff 7e50d6f..3a5d6e3 -- src bin test .github` is empty) — NOT the 7e50d6f the README cites. The README's own rule ('the matrix run for the push that carried the last change to those paths') selects 7e50d6f uniquely and is correct. No guard reads the history file's prose, so nothing catches the disagreement. Fix is one line: quote the README's rule verbatim instead of restating it. Q-10.

The run overshot stop_at by 25.5h — and the FIRST diagnosis of why, written earlier this same cycle, was WRONG and is corrected here. It said 'the pacer produced no cycle'. The pacer log says otherwise: between 2026-08-20T18:59:48Z and 2026-08-22T16:04:02Z it fired faithfully every ~5 minutes and SPAWNED 504 cycles. 503 of them completed; ALL 503 died in ~380ms with HTTP 429, `You've hit your weekly limit · resets Aug 24, 5am (UTC)`, before their first turn. Zero other failure causes — the classification is exhaustive, not a sample. This is precisely L-037's FIRST clause re-observed: a spawned conductor that dies on a usage-limit error before its first turn is invisible to limp mode, because limp needs a session alive enough to run the tier probe, so the SPAWNER must set the limp flag itself on a usage-shaped launch failure instead of respawning on the same schedule. It does not: swarm-pacer.sh logs `cycle-failed` and retries at the same cadence, burning 504 spawns against a wall. The runfile's own last probe had already recorded weekly_used_pct: 100. Human item, and note the correction cost: a liveness check on the pacer (the fix the wrong diagnosis implied) would have PASSED throughout — the pacer was alive; what was dead was every session it started.
